anchorData:
BALLOON AND HAIR (Lesson 1 class activity): Latex balloon, 25 cm diameter when inflated, rubbed on dry hair for 20 strokes (about 10 seconds). Hair strands rise and follow the balloon up to about 5 cm away. Balloon then sticks to a painted classroom wall for about 3 minutes (range 2 to 5 minutes on a dry day, ~35% relative humidity). Torn paper pieces (about 1 cm x 1 cm, mass about 0.01 g each) jump up to the balloon from a desk when it is held about 2 cm above them. Some pieces then fall off again after touching the balloon. Two balloons each rubbed on hair and hung on separate threads push apart (repel); a rubbed balloon and a hair-rubbed-balloon-free strand attract. Unrubbed balloon: no effect on hair, wall or paper. On a humid day (about 80% relative humidity, e.g. Mombasa in the rainy season) the balloon sticks for under 30 seconds or not at all. Nairobi dry-season day: relative humidity about 35%; small shock felt after removing a woollen jersey or combing hair, with a faint crackle heard in a dark room.

TRIBOELECTRIC TABLE (Lesson 3), listed from most easily positive to most easily negative: dry human hair (+), glass, perspex (acrylic), wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex rubber balloon (-). Rule: the material higher in the list becomes positive when rubbed with one lower in the list.

RODS AND STRIPS (Lesson 2): a polythene strip rubbed with wool/fur becomes negative; a perspex rod rubbed with silk becomes positive. Results: two polythene strips repel; two perspex rods repel; polythene and perspex attract.

CHARGE VALUES: proton +1.6 x 10^-19 C; electron -1.6 x 10^-19 C; neutron 0 C. A typical rubbed balloon gains about 10^-9 C (1 nC), which is about 6 x 10^9 extra electrons (1 x 10^-9 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 6.25 x 10^9, rounded to 6 x 10^9). A balloon has roughly 10^23 atoms, so only a tiny fraction of electrons moves.

CONDUCTION TEST (Lesson 4), simple circuit with a 3 V cell (two 1.5 V cells in series) and a torch bulb: bulb lights with copper wire, aluminium foil, metal spoon (steel), graphite (pencil lead); bulb does not light with plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, glass rod, dry cotton cloth.

GOLD-LEAF ELECTROSCOPE (Lesson 8): neutral, leaf hangs down at 0 degrees. A rubbed polythene strip (negative) brought near the cap, not touching, makes the leaf rise to about 30 degrees. Touching the strip to the cap leaves the leaf at about 30 degrees after the strip is removed. Touching the cap with a finger (earthing) returns the leaf to 0 degrees. A stronger charge (more rubbing strokes, 40 vs 20) gives about 50 degrees against 30 degrees. Sign test: with the electroscope negatively charged (leaf at about 30 degrees), bringing a negative object near the cap raises the leaf further (above 30 degrees); bringing a positive object near lowers the leaf (below 30 degrees).

DISTRIBUTION (Lesson 7): charge on a hollow metal can collects on the outer surface; a proof-plane touched on the outside of a charged can makes the electroscope leaf rise to about 40 degrees, while touched on the inside it gives 0 degrees. On a pear-shaped or pointed conductor, the proof plane gives the largest reading at the pointed end (about 45 degrees), a smaller reading at the flat end (about 20 degrees).
characters: Learners in class: Wanjiru (Nairobi, notices her hair stands up after combing on dry mornings), Otieno (Kisumu, notices the sticking balloon on the classroom wall), Amina (Mombasa, says it never works at her coastal home during the rainy season, which leads to the humidity discussion), and Kipchoge (Eldoret, asks whether the shock is like lightning). Teacher: Mr Mwangi, runs the demonstrations. Places: Nairobi (dry season, ~35% humidity, shocks from woollen jerseys), Mombasa (humid, ~80%, weak effects), Kisumu (Lake Victoria region; frequent thunderstorms and lightning), Kericho (tea country, high lightning frequency; lightning conductors on buildings). Objects: latex balloon, polythene strip, perspex rod, ebonite rod, silk and wool/fur cloths, paper pieces, gold-leaf electroscope, proof plane, copper wire, metal spoon. Real-world applications: lightning conductors on buildings in Kericho and Kisumu, fuel tankers at Nairobi petrol depots trailing an earthing chain or bonding wire, photocopiers in school offices, electrostatic precipitators at cement factories (e.g. Athi River). Lightning conductor is a pointed metal rod on top of a building joined by thick copper strip to a buried earth plate.
outcome: The balloon gains extra electrons from the hair when rubbed (hair becomes positive, balloon negative) because latex holds electrons more strongly than hair. Hair strands, both positive, repel each other and rise, and are attracted to the negative balloon. The negative balloon sticks to the neutral wall and attracts neutral paper because it induces opposite charge on the nearby surface (the electrons in the wall and paper shift slightly away, leaving the near side positive) so attraction is stronger than repulsion. The charge only leaks away slowly on dry days; on humid days water vapour lets it escape, so the balloon falls quickly. Charges are not created: electrons are transferred, and total charge is conserved. The shock from a jersey is a small spark when built-up charge discharges.
conventions: Use 'electric charge' (symbol Q, unit coulomb, C); nC = 10^-9 C. Positive charge = deficit of electrons; negative = excess of electrons. Only electrons move in solids; protons stay in the nucleus. Never say 'positive charge moved' for solids. 'Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.' A neutral object is attracted to a charged one (by induction), but is not repelled; repulsion is the sure test for charge sign. 'Charging by friction' (L3), 'by contact' (L5), 'by induction' (L6). Contact gives the SAME sign as the charged object; induction gives the OPPOSITE sign. 'Earthing' means connecting a conductor to the ground so electrons can flow to or from the Earth. 'Conductor' has free (delocalised) electrons; 'insulator' has electrons tightly bound. Use 'electroscope' and 'leaf divergence' (angle in degrees). Term 'electrostatic force' for the force between charges; do not use 'static electricity' as an explanation. Use 'discharge' for removing charge. Say 'transfer of electrons', not 'creation of charge'. Balloon is negative and hair is positive in every lesson. Teachers always use dry conditions; humidity explains failures. Use cm, degrees and C. DQB = Driving Question Board. Model = labelled particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper, revised each lesson. The sparks and lightning explanation uses point discharge: charge crowds at points, strong field ionises the air, charge leaks away.

lessonMap.teaches: Observing and describing electrostatic attraction and repulsion without explaining it, and recording questions on the DQB with initial models
lessonMap.buildsOn: No earlier lessons; uses prior knowledge of magnets and everyday experiences like combing hair
lessonMap.usesData: Balloon and hair (20 strokes, hair rises to 5 cm, sticks to wall 3 min, paper jumps at 2 cm, unrubbed balloon does nothing, humid vs dry Nairobi and Mombasa)

lessonMap.teaches: Atomic structure (protons +, electrons -, neutrons 0), neutral atoms and the rule that like charges repel and unlike charges attract
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: two balloons repel and balloon-hair attract questions
lessonMap.usesData: Rods and strips table; charge values of proton, electron, neutron

lessonMap.teaches: Friction transfers electrons from one material to another; the sign of charge depends on the material pair (triboelectric order); charge is conserved
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 and 2: charge signs, repulsion test for sign, balloon and hair observations
lessonMap.usesData: Triboelectric table; balloon gains about 1 nC (6 x 10^9 electrons); balloon negative and hair positive

lessonMap.teaches: Conductors have free electrons that move through the material, insulators do not; testing with a simple circuit
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2 and 3: electrons are the movers; why charge stays on rubbed insulators like the balloon
lessonMap.usesData: Conduction test with 3 V cell and bulb; list of conducting and non-conducting materials

lessonMap.teaches: A conductor touched by a charged object gains the same sign of charge by electron transfer
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3 and 4: electron transfer and free electrons in conductors
lessonMap.usesData: Electroscope touched with negative polythene strip leaves leaf at about 30 degrees; paper pieces that touch the balloon and fall off

lessonMap.teaches: Charge separation (induction) in a conductor or insulator near a charged object, and charging by induction with earthing to give the opposite sign; explains attraction of neutral paper and wall
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3, 4 and 5: electron movement, conductors, contact charging (same sign, to contrast with opposite sign)
lessonMap.usesData: Neutral paper and wall attracted to negative balloon; earthing with finger returns leaf to 0 degrees; Outcome explanation

lessonMap.teaches: Charge resides on the outer surface and is concentrated at points; point discharge explains sparks and lightning conductors
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 4 and 5: mobile charges in conductors repel each other and spread out; earthing from Lesson 6
lessonMap.usesData: Distribution readings: hollow can outside 40 degrees and inside 0 degrees; pointed end 45 degrees and flat end 20 degrees; Nairobi spark shock

lessonMap.teaches: Using a gold-leaf electroscope to detect charge, determine its sign, discharge it, and relate leaf divergence to amount of charge
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 5, 6 and 7: contact, induction and earthing as ways to charge and discharge; charge on the cap and leaf
lessonMap.usesData: Gold-leaf electroscope values: 0, 30 and 50 degrees (20 vs 40 strokes); sign test above or below 30 degrees; finger earthing

lessonMap.teaches: Applying electrostatics to technology (lightning conductors, photocopiers, precipitators, fuel tanker earthing) and writing the final complete explanation of the anchoring phenomenon
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 to 8: all ideas, with Lesson 7 point discharge for lightning conductors and Lesson 6 earthing for tankers
lessonMap.usesData: Characters' applications (Kericho, Kisumu, Nairobi depots, Athi River); Outcome; balloon charge value of 1 nC and humidity data
